At a glance

Best months
April and May for song and returning migrants, September and October for passage, November to February for geese, waders and murmurations
Regions
Northumberland and the Farne IslandsMorecambe Bay and the Cumbrian coastThe Peak District and the PenninesThe Yorkshire coast: Bempton and SpurnThe Wash and the Lincolnshire coastThe Norfolk coast and the BroadsSuffolk and the Essex coastThe Chilterns, the Thames and the London reservoirsKent, Sussex and the south coastThe Somerset Levels and the SevernThe New Forest, Dorset and Poole HarbourCornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly
Itineraries
A London Layover1 dayThe North Norfolk Weekend3 daysSeabird Cities5 daysThe Southwest in Autumn7 daysEngland End to End12 days
Getting around
A hire car reaches every region on this page, and the train reaches Norfolk, the Chilterns, the Yorkshire coast and the West Country on its own

When to Go

The English birding year has three peaks rather than one. Seabirds fill the cliffs from March to July, migration runs along the coasts through August to October, and the estuaries hold their biggest flocks from November to February.

Spring

March to June

Seabirds come back to the ledges in March, summer migrants arrive through April, and by May every woodland is singing from before five in the morning.

Go for Breeding seabirds, full song, and the longest days of the year in the north.

Trade off Rooms cost the most from Easter onward, and island boats need booking weeks ahead in June.

Typical daily average March 3 to 9 °C / 37 to 48 °F, April 4 to 12 °C / 39 to 54 °F, May 7 to 15 °C / 45 to 59 °F, June 10 to 18 °C / 50 to 64 °F

Autumn

July to October

Wader passage builds from July, the coasts fill with migrants through September, and October is when a rarity can turn up almost anywhere.

Go for Big wader counts, seawatching in an onshore blow, and the best chance of a bird from a long way off course.

Trade off Song has stopped, so birds are identified on plumage and call, and the seabird colonies are empty by August.

Typical daily average July 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F, August 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F, September 10 to 17 °C / 50 to 63 °F, October 8 to 13 °C / 46 to 55 °F

Winter

November to February

Geese, swans and waders pack the estuaries, starlings gather over the reedbeds at dusk, and raptors are easy over open ground.

Go for Six figure goose and wader flocks, murmurations, and reserves you have largely to yourself.

Trade off Daylight is short, and the boats to the Farne Islands stop for the winter.

Typical daily average November 5 to 10 °C / 41 to 50 °F, December 3 to 8 °C / 37 to 46 °F, January 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F, February 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F

1 day

A London Layover

London Heathrow (LHR), the Lee Valley or the Thames marshes, London

RSPB Rainham Marshes is twenty minutes from Fenchurch Street by train and sits on the Thames wall. Half a day gets you marsh, reedbed and estuary and back to the airport.

  1. 1Cley next the Sea
  2. 2Titchwell
  3. 3Snettisham

3 days

The North Norfolk Weekend

Norwich (NWI), Cley, Titchwell, Snettisham

The most concentrated run of reserves in England, all on one coast road. Time the last morning for a big tide at Snettisham, which is the finest wader spectacle in the country.

  1. 1Seahouses
  2. 2Bempton
  3. 3Spurn

5 days

Seabird Cities

Newcastle (NCL), the Farne Islands, Bempton, Spurn

Two of the best seabird colonies in Britain and the migration point between them. May to July for the colonies; late August and September if you would rather have Spurn at its best.

  1. 1Poole
  2. 2Glastonbury

The Southwest in Autumn

Exeter (EXT), Dorset, the Somerset Levels, Cornwall, Scilly

Built around the Isles of Scilly in October, when the islands take American vagrants and the mainland run down provides the wader and seawatch days either side.

12 days

England End to End

Newcastle (NCL), Yorkshire, Lincolnshire, Norfolk, Suffolk, Kent, the New Forest, Somerset

The full sweep, north to south, taking the seabird colonies first and finishing on the reedbeds and heaths. Best in May and June, when everything is on territory at once.

Northumberland and the Farne Islands

Basalt seabird islands and a tidal dune coast, ninety minutes north of Newcastle

A dune and castle coast with a cluster of low basalt islands lying offshore. Landing on Inner Farne in June puts you inside an Arctic tern colony that defends itself vigorously, and grey seals haul out on the rocks below.

Look for: Atlantic Puffin, Common Murre, Black-legged Kittiwake, Arctic Tern, Roseate Tern, Common Eider

Parks and reserves: Farne Islands (island reserve), Lindisfarne National Nature Reserve, Coquet Island (island reserve), Newton Pool (reserve)

Stops: , a working harbour and departure point for Farne Islands boat trips, with National Trust landing tickets sold from the quayside kiosk. Puffins and seals close to the boats , a tidal bay inside the Lindisfarne National Nature Reserve, watched free from a roadside pull-in on the A1. Wigeon and pink-footed geese roost across the mudflats in winter , the tidal causeway linking Holy Island to the mainland, open to cross only within the published tide times. Waders and wildfowl feed on the flats it crosses , a working harbour on the Coquet estuary, the departure point for boat trips around Coquet Island, closed to public landing. Roseate and Arctic terns fish offshore in summer , a clifftop and shore path along the Northumberland coast, free to walk between the fishing village of Craster and Dunstanburgh Castle. Eiders bob close inshore and skuas pass offshore , a boat trip and possible landing on Inner Farne, booked through the National Trust kiosk at Seahouses. Arctic terns dive at your head and eiders sit on the path

Visitor centres: National Trust Farne Islands landing point, Seahouses

Also covers: Alnwick, Ashington, Belsay, Brunton House & Cottages, England, Folly Farm, Hepple Whitefield, Holy Island, Kirkharle, Lowick, Nunnykirk, Rothbury, The Harbour, Tyne & Wear, Wales

Also watch for: The Farne Islands hold one of England's largest grey seal colonies, with pups born on the rocks between October and December. Harbour porpoises and, in late summer, minke whales are seen from the boats, and Atlantic grey seals often surface right alongside them.

Morecambe Bay and the Cumbrian coast

Tidal saltmarsh, shingle spit and sandstone sea cliff around the shores of Cumbria

Two great tidal bays either side of the Cumbrian coast, with the largest reedbed in northwest England behind one of them. Morecambe Bay lifts wader flocks off the sand on a rising tide in numbers that are hard to take in.

Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Bearded Reedling, Western Marsh Harrier, Red Knot, Barnacle Goose, Common Murre

Parks and reserves: Arnside and Silverdale National Landscape, Lake District National Park, Solway Coast National Landscape

Stops: , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and reedbed hides, an entry fee for non-members, open every day of the year. Bittern, marsh harrier and bearded reedling in the reeds , an RSPB reserve on a former iron ore works beside the Duddon estuary, walked from the car park at any time. Terns, eider and wintering wildfowl on the lagoon , a Cumbria Wildlife Trust reserve at the tip of Walney Island, reached from the car park, a small fee for non-members. Grey seals haul out on the shingle spit , an RSPB reserve on the Solway Firth saltmarsh, walked from the car park and hide, open every day without charge. Barnacle geese and golden plover winter on the merse , a stretch of the Morecambe Bay shoreline reached from a roadside car park at the end of Hest Bank Lane. Waders and wildfowl gather here on the incoming tide , an RSPB and United Utilities reserve above the reservoir in the Lake District, walked from the car park at Mardale Head. Ring ouzel and curlew breed on the fells above , an RSPB reserve on Cumbria's only stretch of cliff coastline, walked along a clifftop path from the car park in St Bees. Guillemots, razorbills and kittiwakes nest on the ledges

Visitor centres: RSPB Leighton Moss Visitor Centre, South Walney Nature Reserve (Cumbria Wildlife Trust)

Also covers: Blackpool, Kendal, Lancashire, Lancaster, Penrith, Powfoot, Preston, Ravenglass, Tebay, The Old Station Building, Wigton, Windermere, Wrea Green

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the shingle at South Walney and pup there between October and December, while natterjack toads call from the dune slacks of the Solway coast on warm nights in May and June. Red squirrels still hold on in the oakwoods around Haweswater, one of Cumbria's last strongholds for the species.

Mr & Mrs Smith

A dream come true for the design minded and adventurous epicures, The Forest Side hotel will convince even the most unwavering urbanites to slow down and stay a night (or three) in the Lake District. The draw? A thoughtful renovation of a gorgeous Gothic mansion, during which original Victorian fireplaces were saved and once robust gardens were restored. Fluffy Herdwick sheep graze on the grounds, the restaurant serves some of the best food in the Lake District, and the interiors are just right

The Peak District and the Pennines

Blanket bog, gritstone edge and upland limestone, within reach of Manchester, Sheffield and Leeds

Blanket bog, gritstone edge and limestone dale along the spine of England, within an hour of several large cities. This is where the breeding waders and the moorland birds are, and where the walking is the point.

Look for: Red Grouse, Eurasian Curlew, European Golden Plover, Ring Ouzel, Black Grouse, Merlin

Parks and reserves: Peak District National Park, Yorkshire Dales National Park, North Pennines National Landscape, Forest of Bowland National Landscape

Stops: , an open gritstone moor above the Derwent reservoirs, walked from roadside car parks at any time. Ring ouzel, merlin and red grouse on the heather and tors , a National Trust and RSPB partnership reserve on Sheffield's edge, walked from free car parks at Curbar Gap or Big Moor. Curlew and ring ouzel over the heather , a wooded reservoir valley in the Peak District, walked from the Errwood car park, open at any time. Ring ouzel and curlew on the moor edges above the water , a National Nature Reserve in the North Pennines, reached from Bowlees Visitor Centre or across the Cow Green Reservoir causeway. Golden plover, curlew and black grouse on the limestone moor , a National Nature Reserve and England's highest marl lake, reached from the National Trust car park in the Yorkshire Dales. Curlew and snipe breed on the fen around it , a limestone amphitheatre in the Yorkshire Dales, reached on foot from a free car park, open at any time. Peregrine falcons nest on the cliff face most summers , a moorland valley in the Forest of Bowland, walked from a roadside car park in the Trough of Bowland. One of England's best places for breeding merlin

Visitor centres: Bowlees Visitor Centre, Yorkshire Dales National Park Centre, Malham

Also covers: Alton, Ashbourne, Ashford in the Water, Barnard Castle, Barnsley, Bolton, Bradford, Burgess House, Burnley, Bury, Buxton, Chatsworth Settlement Trustees, Cheadle, Chesham, Cheshire, Chesterfield, Cumbria, Darlington, Derby, Didžioji Britanija, Durham, Grindleford, Harmby, Harrogate, Hathersage, Hawes, Holmes Chapel, Ilam, Kilnsey, Knutsford, Lancashire, Lanchester, Leigh, Macclesfield, Masham, Matlock, Northumberland, Oldham, Paris, Patrick, Rochdale, Rowsley, Royston, Salford, Skipton, Springwood, Staffordshire, Staindrop, Stockport, Stoke-on-Trent, Storbritannia, Storbritannien, Swinton, Velika Britanija, West Bretton, Woolley, Worsley, Yorkshire

Also watch for: Mountain hares still wear white winter coats on the high moors above Derwent Edge from December to February, and red deer graze the bracken slopes of the Eastern Moors through autumn. Upper Teesdale's sugar limestone grassland flowers with spring gentian and globeflower in May and June, a rarity found almost nowhere else in England.

Mr & Mrs Smithi-escape

Overlooking North Yorkshire’s moors is Middleton Lodge Estate. King Street Townhouse

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smith

From above, Manchester is a heartbreaker; King Street Townhouse hotel’s south-facing rooms and suites, and rooftop pool overlook the city’s ruggedly handsome skyline – a muddle of spires and glass monoliths dominated by the Town Hall and sci-fi-esque Beetham Tower. Below, the excitement of this music-obsessed, football-mad city is palpable – but within, the chandelier-lit tavern, tea lounge and refined mod-Brit rooms create a calm sanctum for grown-up Madchester kids to refuel in.

The Yorkshire coast: Bempton and Spurn

Chalk cliffs and a shifting sand spit, gannets and migration drama on the East Yorkshire coast

Chalk cliffs at one end and a shifting sand spit at the other, an hour apart. Bempton gives eye level views of England's only mainland gannet colony, and Spurn funnels migration into a strip of land a few hundred metres wide.

Look for: Northern Gannet, Black-legged Kittiwake, Atlantic Puffin, Common Murre, Razorbill, Little Tern

Parks and reserves: RSPB Bempton Cliffs (RSPB reserve), Flamborough Cliffs Nature Reserve, Spurn National Nature Reserve, Kilnsea Wetlands Nature Reserve

Stops: , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and a parking charge, its clifftop platforms giving eye level views onto the ledges. England's only mainland gannet colony, with kittiwakes, puffins and guillemots , a Yorkshire Wildlife Trust reserve with a small seas centre and free access, a clifftop path leading out from the beach. Auks and gannets pass the headland on the way to Bempton , a Yorkshire Wildlife Trust reserve with hides reached from a roadside car park, free to visit. Migrant waders and wildfowl on freshwater scrapes behind the sea wall , a Yorkshire Wildlife Trust visitor centre with an entry fee, the gateway to the reserve and home to the bird observatory's ringing station. A first stop for finding out what has been seen that morning , a fenced lagoon on the beach between Kilnsea and Easington, watched from the path with free access. Yorkshire's only little tern colony, wardened through the summer , the tip of a narrow shifting sand spit within the National Nature Reserve, reached on foot along the sea defence, free to visit. Migrating seabirds pass close by the point in autumn winds

Visitor centres: RSPB Bempton Cliffs Visitor Centre, Spurn Discovery Centre

Also covers: England, Northern Ireland, Pickering, Rosedale Abbey

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the sandbanks at the mouth of the Humber, visible from Spurn's point in good numbers through the winter. Harbour porpoises can be watched offshore from the Bempton clifftop through summer, and migrant moths and butterflies gather around Spurn's bushes each autumn.

Saltmoore

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smithi-escape

Sartorial Saltmoore shines like a beacon between North Yorkshire’s heather-carpeted moors and rugged coastline. This picture-perfect retreat brings together a fetching setting — a lake-stamped estate that’s a stroll from Sandsend Beach — and enviable, romance-inspiring interiors. A holistic spa restores with a view-blessed pool and pink-salt sauna, and a clutch of eateries whip up superlative, seasonal dining. Despite its saline setting (and name), Saltmoore hits all the sweet spots.

The Wash and the Lincolnshire coast

Saltmarsh, mudflats and reedbed around the Wash and the Humber, on the open Lincolnshire coast

A vast square bay of sand and mud with reserves along its southern and western edges, running north into dune and saltmarsh. Wader and wildfowl counts here are among the highest anywhere in Britain.

Look for: Red Knot, Bar-tailed Godwit, Pied Avocet, Common Shelduck, Western Marsh Harrier, Twite

Parks and reserves: RSPB Frampton Marsh (RSPB reserve), RSPB Freiston Shore (RSPB reserve), Gibraltar Point National Nature Reserve, Far Ings National Nature Reserve, RSPB Blacktoft Sands (RSPB reserve)

Stops: , an RSPB reserve on the edge of the Wash, a visitor centre and screens looking over freshwater scrapes, free to enter and open every day. Avocets, knots and passage ruff , an RSPB reserve of managed realignment saltmarsh on the Wash, walked freely along the seawall from a free car park. Shelduck, brent geese and huge wader roosts , a National Nature Reserve of dunes, saltmarsh and freshwater scrapes, with a visitor centre and free trails, open every day with no booking. Migrant passerines and wintering wildfowl , a National Nature Reserve on a military range, walked along a roped beach path, free and open outside range hours. Grey seals pup in November and December, plus shorebirds , a National Nature Reserve of old clay pits beside the Humber, a visitor centre and hides reached on foot, free to enter every day. Bearded reedlings, bitterns and marsh harriers , an RSPB reserve holding the largest tidal reedbed on the Humber, six hides reached along a level path, entry fee for non-members. Marsh harriers, bearded reedlings and passage waders , a managed realignment wetland where the Trent, Ouse and Humber meet, open access with a viewing platform and hides, free to visit. Golden plover flocks and hunting hen harriers , a National Nature Reserve of dunes and damp slacks on the open Lincolnshire coast, free access along boardwalk trails with no booking. Migrant warblers and flocks of twite in winter

Visitor centres: RSPB Frampton Marsh Visitor Centre, Gibraltar Point Visitor Centre, Far Ings Visitor Centre

Also covers: Aspen Farm, Avalon, Cambridgeshire, Church Farm, Council House, Dean House, Deepdale Farm, England, Gainsborough, Grimsby, Haven Cottage, Heath Farm, Hull, Lincoln, Louth, Milestone House, Moat House, North Killingholme, Orchard Farm, School House, The Barn, The Old Station House, Wales, Yew Tree Cottage, York

Also watch for: Grey seals gather to give birth on the beach at Donna Nook every November and December, with several thousand pups born along the roped viewing path. Brown hares box across the fields behind the sea banks in early spring, and water voles can be seen along the ditches at Far Ings and Frampton Marsh through the summer.

The Norfolk coast and the Broads

Shingle coast, reed fen and open water, two and a half hours from London by train to Norwich or King's Lynn

Shingle, saltmarsh and grazing marsh along the north coast, with reed fen and open water inland. More reserves sit within an hour of each other here than anywhere else in Britain, and the winter spectacle is on a European scale.

Look for: Pied Avocet, Eurasian Bittern, Eurasian Spoonbill, Western Marsh Harrier, Common Crane, Bearded Reedling

Parks and reserves: Broads National Park, Holkham National Nature Reserve, Titchwell Marsh RSPB reserve, Cley Marshes, Norfolk Wildlife Trust (reserve), Hickling Broad National Nature Reserve

Stops: , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and an entry fee for non-members, walked on a level path and boardwalk out to the beach. Avocet, marsh harrier and bearded reedling across three habitats in one walk , a Norfolk Wildlife Trust reserve with a visitor centre, hides and an entry fee, the oldest county Wildlife Trust reserve in Britain. Avocet and spoonbill on the scrapes, bittern booming from the reedbed in spring , a National Nature Reserve of dune, pine woodland and saltmarsh, walked freely from several free car parks along the coast road. Pink-footed geese in winter, spoonbills nesting in the pines, a huge wader roost , an unstaffed RSPB reserve reached by a roadside car park and a short walk along the sea wall, free to enter. Tens of thousands of knot and other waders lifting off the Wash on a rising tide , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and entry fee, walked on trails through reedbed, wet woodland and orchid meadow beside the River Yare. Marsh harrier, bittern and, on a good day, a swallowtail butterfly , a Norfolk Wildlife Trust National Nature Reserve with a visitor centre, hides and a guided boat trip, entry fee for non-members. Marsh harrier, bittern and the best chance in the Broads of common crane , a National Trust site with a windpump, car park and a network of free footpaths across the marshes. The centre of the reintroduced common crane population on the Broads, marsh harrier overhead

Visitor centres: Cley Marshes Visitor Centre, Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Titchwell Marsh Visitor Centre, RSPB, Hickling Broad Visitor Centre, Norfolk Wildlife Trust

Also covers: Fakenham, Suffolk, Suite 7, The Links

Also watch for: Common and grey seals haul out at Blakeney Point all year, with grey seal pups born from October to January. Chinese water deer graze the Broads reedbeds and marshes year round, and swallowtail butterflies, found nowhere else in Britain, fly over the fens from late May to July.

Suffolk and the Essex coast

Reedbed, heath and shingle on a low estuary coast, two hours from London

Reedbed, heath and shingle running down to a low estuary coast. Minsmere is the reserve that made birdwatching popular in Britain, and the shingle at Orford Ness carries plants and birds found in very few other places.

Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Bearded Reedling, Pied Avocet, Western Marsh Harrier, Eurasian Spoonbill

Parks and reserves: RSPB Minsmere (RSPB reserve), Orford Ness National Nature Reserve

Stops: , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and an entry fee for non-members, reached on paths through reedbed and heath to the beach. Bitterns, avocets and marsh harriers year round , a National Trust heathland reserve beside the beach, entered freely from its own car park. Dartford warblers, stonechats and nightjars on the heather in summer , a shingle spit reached only by a National Trust ferry booked in advance from Orford quay. Avocets, terns and rare shingle plants among former military buildings , an Essex Wildlife Trust reserve with a visitor centre beside a working reservoir, watched from hides and a causeway. Tens of thousands of wintering wildfowl , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre on the Thames path east of London, walked on boardwalks across grazing marsh. Bearded reedlings, marsh harriers and water voles

Visitor centres: RSPB Minsmere Visitor Centre, RSPB Rainham Marshes Visitor Centre

Also covers: Castle Hill, Colchester, Dartford, Fawkham, Felixstowe, Grays, Ipswich, Kent, Marks Tey, Southend-on-Sea, Woodbridge, Yaxley

Also watch for: Adders and silver studded blue butterflies bask on the heather at Dunwich Heath and Dungeness through the summer months, and water voles work the ditches at Rainham Marshes from spring onward. Common seals haul out on the sandbanks of the Blackwater and Colne estuaries near Abberton, best watched as the tide falls.

The Chilterns, the Thames and the London reservoirs

Chalk escarpment, flooded gravel pit and reservoir on the edge of London

Chalk escarpment, gravel pit and working reservoir within reach of central London by train. Red kites released here in the eighties are now a common sight over the hills, and the wetlands hold bittern and marsh harrier. The Thames itself runs through the middle of it, and the reservoirs beside the river hold the wildfowl the region is worth a winter day for.

Look for: Red Kite, Eurasian Hobby, Little Ringed Plover, Common Snipe, Western Marsh Harrier, Eurasian Bittern

Parks and reserves: Chilterns National Landscape, Lee Valley Regional Park (reserve), Colne Valley Regional Park (reserve)

Stops: , an RSPB reserve on reclaimed grazing marsh in Oxfordshire, walked along a bridleway from the car park, open every day without charge. Marsh harrier, bittern and lapwing over the reedbed , a Wildlife Trust reserve in a former chalk quarry near Tring, with a visitor centre, a small entry fee for non-members. Lapwing, snipe and little ringed plover on the pits , a National Trust chalk hill in the Chilterns, with a free car park at Christmas Common, open at any time. Red kites wheel overhead most days of the year , a WWT visitor centre and wetland reserve on former reservoirs at Barnes, with hides, an entry fee for non-members. Bittern, marsh harrier and wintering wildfowl on the lagoons , a working reservoir split into two basins by a causeway, watched from the public footpath along the top. Rare gulls and wintering diving ducks gather on the water , an RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and boardwalk beside the River Lea, an entry fee for non-members, open every day. Kingfisher, common tern and bittern on the reedbed , four canal feeder reservoirs on the Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire border, walked on public paths from car parks at Wilstone and Marsworth. Hobbies hunt dragonflies over the water in summer

Visitor centres: WWT London Wetland Centre, RSPB Rye Meads Visitor Centre, College Lake Visitor Centre (BBOWT)

Also covers: Ascot, Banbury, Basingstoke, Bedfordshire, Belgravia, Berkshire, Bicester, Blunsdon, Borehamwood, Bracknell, Brentford, Buckinghamshire, Cambridge, Colnbrook, Cranfield, Cromer, Donnington, Elstree, Enterprise House, Eversley, Eynsham, Farnborough, First Floor, Gibraltar, Hatfield Heath, Hayes, Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, Hyde Park Corner, International House, Kings Langley, Knightsbridge, Londen, Londona, Londres, Londýn, Luton, Maidenhead, Marlow, Middlesex, Milton Hill, Milton Keynes, Newbury, Old Barn, Oliver, Oxford, Reading, Rotherwick, Silverstone, Slough, Spring Grove, Stevenage, Surrey, Swindon, Taplow, Thame, The Oaks, The Warren, Towcester, Tring, Uxbridge, Victoria, Windsor, Wokingham

Also watch for: Fallow and muntjac deer move through the beechwoods of the Chilterns escarpment all year, and silver-spotted skippers and chalkhill blue butterflies fly over the flower-rich turf of Watlington Hill in July and August. Otters have returned to the rivers and lakes around Tring and Rye Meads after decades of absence, most often spotted at dawn or dusk.

L'oscar

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smith

Inspired by turn-of-the-century decadence and London’s dandiest playwright, L’oscar is a hotel that’s given to theatrics and partial to pleasure. Built in 1903, the Grade-II listed building was revived by designer Jacques Garcia, who restored marble fireplaces and oak-panelled walls, and added a seven-storey chandelier and a bar that glows like molten lava. Oscar Wilde thought that moderation was a fatal thing; seen through his eyes, L’oscar might just be London’s most life-affirming hotel.

Kent, Sussex and the south coast

Shingle spits, grazing marsh and chalk cliffs across Kent and Sussex, within two hours of London

Shingle, grazing marsh and chalk headland along the Channel, within two hours of London. Dungeness is where a rarity can turn up in any month, and the Sheppey marshes hold wintering raptors in numbers.

Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Western Marsh Harrier, Bearded Reedling, Pied Avocet, Hen Harrier, Eurasian Hobby

Parks and reserves: Dungeness National Nature Reserve, Elmley Nature Reserve, Rye Harbour Nature Reserve, Pagham Harbour Local Nature Reserve, RSPB Pulborough Brooks (RSPB reserve)

Stops: , an RSPB reserve on Denge Beach's shingle, with a visitor centre and hides around old gravel pits, free to enter with paid parking. Bitterns, marsh harriers and hunting hobbies , a working bird observatory beside the lighthouses, open to visitors for ringing demonstrations and the daily sightings log, no need to book. Migrant thrushes, chats and falls of warblers , a privately run reserve on the Isle of Sheppey, entered along a mile-long farm track across grazing marsh, small entry charge, no booking needed. Lapwings, redshanks and hunting hen harriers , a Kent Wildlife Trust reserve on the Swale, a short circuit of scrapes and a sea wall walked free from a small car park. Avocets, black-tailed godwits and passage waders , a National Nature Reserve of shingle and grazing marsh, with a Discovery Centre and a network of free hides, open every day. Breeding terns, avocets and wintering wildfowl , a local nature reserve around a tidal harbour, walked along the seawall path from car parks at Church Norton and Sidlesham Ferry. Brent geese, bar-tailed godwits and wintering waders , an RSPB reserve on the Arun floodplain, with a visitor centre, cafe and trails through wet grassland, entry fee for non-members. Wintering lapwings, wigeon and hobbies hunting over summer , a chalk headland on open access land above England's highest chalk cliffs, free to walk with no booking. Peregrines, ravens and passage migrants along the cliff edge

Visitor centres: RSPB Dungeness Visitor Centre, RSPB Pulborough Brooks Visitor Centre

Also covers: Borough Farm, Brighton, Buxsted, Canterbury, Cleveland, Dover, Durham, East Cliff, Essex, Farnham, Gatwick, Hampshire, Lenham, Little Horsted, Maidstone, Middlesbrough, Newhill Farm, Northumberland, Portsmouth, Ramsgate, Surrey, The Waterfront, Tonbridge, Uckfield, Yarm, Yorkshire

Also watch for: Common and grey seals haul out on the shingle at Rye Harbour and can often be seen offshore from Dungeness through the year. Adders and common lizards warm themselves on the shingle banks from March, and Dungeness holds one of the richest populations of moths and beetles found anywhere in Britain.

The Pig in the South Downs

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smith

Tucked neatly down a country lane not far from Arundel, the Pig in the South Downs is a porkin' corker, comprising a manor house and series of artfully upcycled outbuildings. The menu at the lawn-side restaurant keeps things local — even more than usual from the kitchen garden, owing to its bounteous proportions. In a Pig first, there's a verdant vineyard, too, so if you squint a little on a sunny day, you'll think you've trotted off to some quiet corner of Provence.

The Pig in the Wall

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smith

A Georgian townhouse and former pub, The Pig in the Wall is a charming stay for anyone who needs to be in or around Southampton, the closest city to the New Forest. A boutique hotel with a rustic soul right in the mediaeval city walls, near to the cruise terminals on Southampton Water, this little sister to the celebrated restaurant with rooms in the New Forest has a corking deli counter that would make its porcine country-house sibling proud.

The Ropemaker, Emsworth

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smith

The Ropemaker, Emsworth is a palate-tempting pub with rooms, near cultural Chichester and West Sussex beaches, that will pull you into its coastal embrace. Brightly hued bedrooms are kitted out with Roberts radios and Bramley sleep spray, but a French-nodding dinner at the Raymond Blanc-approved restaurant — or a couple of house cocktails at the bar or on the terrace — has a similar soporific effect. The whole clan (pooches included) will know the ropes in no time.

The Swan Inn Fittleworth

· Luxury

Mr & Mrs Smith

A 14th-century coaching inn, The Swan Inn Fittleworth has the bowed-beam ceilings and autograph-heavy visitors’ books to prove its storied credentials. Yet this polished pub with rooms is no museum piece. At its heart is provenance-proud pub fare and Sussex-sourced tipples. Bedrooms, including family- and pet-friendly options, offer refined rusticity, too. And the verdant South Downs are on your doorstep. Country lovers, take note.

The Somerset Levels and the Severn

Restored peat wetland reedbeds and the tidal Severn, roughly two hours from London by train to Castle Cary or Bridgwater

Restored peat wetland below the Mendips and a vast tidal estuary west of it. The Levels now hold bitterns and a winter starling murmuration that draws crowds, and the Severn takes wild swans and geese from the Arctic.

Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Great Egret, Eurasian Hobby, Common Crane, Tundra Swan, Eurasian Spoonbill

Parks and reserves: Shapwick Heath National Nature Reserve, Westhay Moor Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve), Bridgwater Bay National Nature Reserve, Severn Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve)

Stops: , an RSPB reedbed reserve with free access from a roadside car park near Ashcott. Booming bitterns, hunting hobbies and, in winter, huge starling murmurations , a National Nature Reserve on former peat workings, walked freely from the Sweet Track car park. Bitterns, great white egrets and otters along the ditches , a Somerset Wildlife Trust reserve on flooded peat diggings, with a paid car park off the Westhay road. Bitterns, otters and a vast winter starling roost , a Somerset Wildlife Trust reserve of flooded fields and reedbed, walked freely from a car park on Lady's Drove. Wintering wigeon and teal, egrets, and otters from the Tower Hide , a WWT working wetland of saltmarsh and freshwater pools, open free of charge with paths from the visitor car park. Avocets, spoonbills and wintering wildfowl on the Severn shore , a WWT wetland centre with an entry fee, hides and heated lookouts over managed pools and the Severn saltings. The best place in England for wintering Bewick's swans , an open sea wall walked from a roadside parking spot near the old ferry crossing at New Passage. Wading birds and wildfowl on the tide across the Severn , an RSPB woodland reserve with a car park and hide, overlooking the closed West Sedgemoor marsh. Herons breeding in the wood and, in winter, reintroduced common cranes

Visitor centres: Avalon Marshes Centre, WWT Slimbridge Wetland Centre, WWT Steart Marshes Visitor Centre

Also covers: Almondsbury, Avon, Bath, Bibury, Bristol, Brockhampton, Cardiff, Cheltenham, Chepstow, Coleford, Derry Hill, Fiddler's Green, Frampton Cotterell, Gloucester, Langridge, Loxton, Malmesbury, Malvern, Newport, Penarth CF64, South Cerney, Taunton

Also watch for: Otters and water voles work the drainage rhynes and are most reliably seen at dawn, while roe deer graze the willow carr year round. Adders bask on the drier tracks of Shapwick Heath in March and April, and dragonflies including the hairy dragonfly and four-spotted chaser fill the reedbeds from May to August.

The New Forest, Dorset and Poole Harbour

Heathland, harbour and chalk coast around Bournemouth and Weymouth, under two hours from London by train to Poole or Weymouth

Ancient wood pasture and open heath running down to a shallow harbour and a chalk headland. The heaths carry Dartford warblers and nightjars, and Portland Bill logs whatever is passing offshore.

Look for: Dartford Warbler, European Nightjar, Osprey, Eurasian Spoonbill, Sandwich Tern, Pied Avocet

Parks and reserves: New Forest National Park, Poole Harbour Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve), Durlston National Nature Reserve, Dorset and East Devon Coast World Heritage Site (reserve)

Stops: , an open heath in the New Forest, walked freely from a Forestry England car park at Acres Down. One of England's few reliable spots for honey buzzard and hobby overhead , an RSPB heathland reserve with a visitor centre, café and an entry fee, on the shore of Poole Harbour. Dartford warblers, nightjars and spoonbills, plus reintroduced ospreys overhead , a Dorset Wildlife Trust island in Poole Harbour, reached by ferry from Poole Quay with an entry fee. Terns and avocets on the lagoon, red squirrels in the woods , a working headland with a bird observatory in the old lower lighthouse, staffed by volunteer ringers. The top seawatching point on the Dorset coast for shearwaters and skuas , an RSPB reedbed reserve in central Weymouth, with a discovery centre and free access from the bus and rail stations. Bearded tits, bitterns and marsh harriers beside the shops , an RSPB wetland reserve on the edge of Weymouth, with free access from a seafront car park. Bearded tits and Cetti's warblers, and migrant waders on passage , a Dorset Council country park and National Nature Reserve on the Purbeck cliffs, with a castle visitor centre and free access. Breeding guillemots and razorbills below, and seabirds passing , a headland and local nature reserve at the mouth of Christchurch Harbour, walked freely from a large car park. A well watched migration point for warblers and passing seabirds

Visitor centres: RSPB Arne visitor centre, Durlston Castle, Wild Weymouth Discovery Centre, Radipole Lake

Also covers: Amesbury, Beaulieu, Burley, Devon, Eastleigh, Fareham, Fordingbridge, Hampshire, Hythe, Isle of Wight, Itchen Stoke, Lyndhurst, New Milton, Nr Tisbury, Portland, Ringwood, Southampton, Stockbridge, Wick Ferry, Wiltshire, Winchester

Also watch for: Sika deer roam the heath and reedbeds around Poole Harbour and are most vocal during their rut in October, while Brownsea Island holds one of southern England's few surviving red squirrel populations. Adders and sand lizards bask on the Dorset heaths in spring, and grey seals haul out on the ledges below Durlston through the year.

Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly

Granite headlands, tidal estuaries and an offshore archipelago, from Penzance out to islands reached by ferry or plane

A long granite peninsula ending in an Atlantic archipelago twenty eight miles past Land's End. Scilly is where Britain's rarities arrive each October, and the south Devon estuaries hold cirl buntings and wintering waders.

Look for: Manx Shearwater, European Storm Petrel, Sooty Shearwater, Red-billed Chough, Cirl Bunting, Eurasian Spoonbill

Parks and reserves: Isles of Scilly Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (National Landscape), Cornwall National Landscape, West Penwith, Lundy Marine Conservation Zone (reserve), Exe Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve)

Stops: , an RSPB reedbed reserve behind Marazion beach, walked freely from nearby pay and display parking. Cornwall's largest reedbed, holding bitterns and, in autumn, huge starling murmurations over Mount's Bay , an RSPB estuary reserve at Ryan's Field off Chenhalls Road in Hayle, open at all times. Up to eighteen thousand ducks and waders on the mud in winter , a fishing cove below the coast path near Land's End, reached from a National Trust car park, free to walk. Cornwall's classic autumn watchpoint for rare migrants and passing seabirds , a National Trust headland, England's most westerly point, with open clifftop paths and no fee to walk them. Choughs on the cliffs and a fine seawatching spot for shearwaters , an archipelago of five inhabited islands reached by ferry from Penzance or plane from Land's End, walked freely on open paths. Britain's foremost autumn magnet for rare migrant birds , an RSPB wetland reserve beside the Exe estuary, with free access and a car park off the old Exeter canal path. Wintering brent geese, wigeon and hunting peregrines , an RSPB hide and viewing platform on the Exe estuary at Topsham, free to visit at any time. Avocets, godwits and, some winters, a wintering spoonbill , a granite island in the Bristol Channel, reached by the MS Oldenburg from Bideford or Ilfracombe, with a landing fee on arrival. England's largest Manx shearwater colony and breeding puffins

Visitor centres: Isles of Scilly Wildlife Trust, Cornwall Wildlife Trust, RSPB Exe Estuary reserves office, Darts Farm

Also covers: Blackawton, Braunton, Bude, Budleigh Salterton, Cornwal, Exeter, Exmouth, Falmouth, Higher East Leigh, Lynton, Oakford, Paignton, Princetown, Reed Hall, Sidmouth EX10, Smallbrook, Somerset, St Martin, Torquay, West Down

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on rocks around the Isles of Scilly and Godrevy year round, with pups born on the quieter beaches from August to November, and Atlantic common dolphins and harbour porpoises are regularly seen from the Porthgwarra and Land's End coast path. Basking sharks pass close inshore off west Cornwall from May to July, feeding at the surface on summer plankton blooms.

Birding Community

English birding is unusually well organised, and several of these bodies own the reserves on this page or take the bookings for the boats. Find a birding organisation near you in our worldwide directory

Alongside the national bodies below, England has 43 local bird clubs across 42 regions. They run the walks and the counts, and most of them welcome visitors. See every English club by region.

RSPB BirdLife in the UK, and the owner of a great many of the reserves on this page. Membership pays for itself quickly if you plan to visit more than a handful. Visit BTO The British Trust for Ornithology, which runs the national surveys and ringing scheme, and publishes the population figures behind this page. Visit The Wildlife Trusts Forty-six county trusts owning many of the smaller reserves named here, including Spurn and much of the Somerset Levels. Visit WWT The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust, which runs Slimbridge on the Severn and several other wetland centres. Visit BirdGuides The national sightings and rarity service, and how English birders find out what has turned up where. Visit

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in England?

May and June for seabird colonies, heathland and full song together. September and October for passage on both coasts, and October on Scilly for American vagrants. December to February for waders and wildfowl on the estuaries, which is when the biggest counts happen.

Where should I go for a first English birding trip?

North Norfolk. Cley, Titchwell, Holkham and Snettisham sit along twenty-five miles of one coast road, and between them they cover reedbed, saltmarsh, freshwater scrape and tidal flat. It works in every month of the year and there is more written about it than anywhere else in England.

Do I need a car?

Less than in most countries. Rainham, Dungeness, Bempton, Leighton Moss and Slimbridge are all reachable by train and a short walk or taxi, and the Coasthopper bus runs the whole north Norfolk coast road. A car still helps in the New Forest, the Peak District and the Somerset Levels, where reserves are spread out and buses are thin.

Which English birds are hard to find elsewhere in Britain?

Dartford Warbler, Nightingale, Turtle Dove, Stone-curlew, Cirl Bunting and Bittern are all far more findable in England than in Scotland or Wales, and most of them are effectively confined to the south. Cirl Bunting in particular is down to south Devon and a small reintroduced Cornish population.

Is Scilly worth it in October?

If you want the chance of an American passerine, yes, and nowhere else in Britain compares. It is a long journey and the weather decides everything, so go for the islands and treat the rarities as the bonus rather than the plan.

What is the best wader spectacle in England?

Snettisham on the Wash, on a spring tide of about 8 metres. The rising water pushes tens of thousands of knot and godwit off the mud and onto the pits behind the shingle, and the flocks move as one. Check the tide tables before you commit to a date.

Can I see Red Kite easily?

Yes. The Chilterns reintroduction has been so successful that kites are now a normal roadside bird along the M40 and across much of central southern England. No reserve is needed.

How much does an English birding trip cost?

Accommodation is the largest line and varies enormously by season and region. Almost every reserve on this page is free to walk or costs a small entry, and RSPB or Wildlife Trust membership covers most of the charged ones.

Do I need to book the island boats?

For the Farne Islands in June and July, yes, well ahead. Scilly flights and the Scillonian also fill in October. Bempton, Spurn and the mainland reserves need no booking at all.
